title: Which Listed Companies Have China's Three Internet Giants Invested In So Far?
excerpt: One company could well end up with Tencent, Baidu, Alibaba and Xiaomi all on its shareholder list.
body:
One company could well end up with Tencent, Baidu, Alibaba and Xiaomi all on its shareholder list.

Another US-listed Chinese internet company plans to come home.

eLong, the Nasdaq-listed online travel agency, announced yesterday that its shareholder Tencent had offered to take it private. Tencent proposed to buy every outstanding share except those held by other eLong shareholders such as Trip.com Group and Plateno, turning eLong back into an unlisted company.

In 2011 Tencent paid US$84 million for 15% of eLong. But eLong has done poorly as a listed company: in the second quarter of this year its revenue was only 234 million yuan, and it lost 356 million yuan. Wall Street has been just as discouraging. eLong's share price has fallen 37% from its high in May.

"Around the world, it is an irreversible trend for local companies to list at home, where the consumers and investors who know them best are… If Tencent's take-private of eLong succeeds, eLong will keep growing bigger and stronger, and relisting on the domestic capital market is naturally one of our options," eLong CEO Jiang Hao, who came over from Trip.com Group, wrote in an email to all staff.

That is roughly the calculation facing the dozen or so US-listed Chinese companies that have chosen to come home over the past year: China's stock markets value companies far more generously than America's.

This year a string of US-listed Chinese internet companies, including Momo, Renren, Shanda Games and Qihoo 360, have announced take-private offers in preparation for delisting. Years may pass between announcing a delisting and actually relisting at home. But these companies, and the investors behind them, are all hoping for another round of inflated valuations, and for paper wealth to multiply several times over.

Behind many of these companies, whether already listed in the US or once planning to list there and now dismantling their VIE structures to come home, stand Baidu, Tencent and Alibaba, China's three internet giants. eLong is only the latest in a dense run of investments the three have made over the past two years.

Dozens of companies in China and abroad have now taken money from Alibaba, Tencent and Baidu, gone public, and kept competing on the open market. Some of these ties are purely about financial returns, but many are bound up with the giants' rivalry with one another:

#### **Alibaba's investments in listed companies: 15**

**June 2015: SMG**

On June 4 this year, Alibaba's project with SMG finally came through: the two set up a joint holding company to invest in SMG's China Business Network (Yicai). Once the deal closes, Alibaba will pay 1.2 billion yuan to hold 36.74% of Yicai indirectly, and Yicai's news and data will be fed to platforms such as Alipay and Mobile Taobao. The two are also developing a financial app called "DT" and the hardware that goes with it, yet another product that aims to be "China's Bloomberg."

**March 2015: Enlight Media**

Founded in 1998, Enlight has grown into one of China's largest private media and entertainment groups. In 2014 it released 12 films that together took 3.14 billion yuan at the box office, and its net profit for the year topped 300 million yuan. Early this year Alibaba paid 2.4 billion yuan for 8.8% of this "New Third Board" company. Most further cooperation will happen inside Alibaba Pictures, which now runs independently.

**January 2015: Guangzhou Baiyunshan Pharmaceutical**

In southern China, Baiyunshan is an important drug retail channel, and its steady earnings got it listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange as early as 1997. This was the first investment by Alibaba Health, Alibaba's Hong Kong-listed affiliate, after it changed its name. Investing alongside it was Yunfeng Capital, which manages Alibaba-related capital and investment projects.

**November 2014: Huayi Brothers**

Like Enlight Media, this is a "big" content company listed on the Hong Kong exchange's Growth Enterprise Market. Huayi now rests on what it calls its "new three carriages": its traditional business, live entertainment and games, and internet business. Jack Ma invested in the company personally as early as 2009, and in November 2014 it took another 1.533 billion yuan from Alibaba.

**September 2014: Shiji Information**

You have probably never heard of this listed company. Founded in 1998, it listed on the main board of the Shenzhen Stock Exchange in 2007. It holds more than 90% of China's market for information management systems at five-star hotels. In 2014 Alibaba paid 2.81 billion yuan for 15% of the company so that the system, and the data it connects to, could serve Alibaba's travel business.

**June 2014: Evergrande Football**

On June 30, 2015, Evergrande announced it would spin off its culture business and its football business and file separate applications to list them on the New Third Board. If that succeeds, it could become the first football club in China to be listed and traded, which would seem to vindicate Jack Ma's judgment when he invested in 2014.

**April 2014: Hundsun Technologies**

During the stock market's recent slump, Hundsun's HOMS trading system for private funds was blamed as a main cause of the turmoil. In fact, across every branch of finance, whether stocks, securities, insurance or funds, more than half of the IT trading systems in use come from this company. Hundsun listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange in December 2003 and is now worth about 37 billion yuan. After it took 3.3 billion yuan from Alibaba, the two began a series of joint projects, such as an internet finance product developed recently with Ant Group and China National Investment and Guaranty.

**April 2014: Wasu Media**

In the Hangzhou area, Wasu Media directly controls the cable TV set-top boxes of 2.49 million households. It is also one of the few companies in China that hold an IPTV operating license, an OTT internet TV license and a national integrated operating license for 3G mobile TV. "TBO," the streaming plan Alibaba is due to unveil this August, will draw its content from this large media company, in which Alibaba has invested more than 6.5 billion yuan.

**April 2014: Youku Tudou**

Youku and Tudou, China's two big online video companies, listed separately on Nasdaq in 2010 and 2011, but in 2012 they agreed to merge, creating the country's largest online video platform. High bandwidth and content costs, plus the capital spending needed to improve its business and operations, have since dragged its market value down to US$3.763 billion. Neither Alibaba's investment of as much as US$1.22 billion nor its steady use of video-ad technology to lift the company's revenue has done much good.

**March 2014: Intime Retail**

Before Koubei, Alibaba's strategy for reaching offline commerce had only two entry points: Taodiandian, which delivers takeout to your door, and Intime Department Store, which does quite well in the Yangtze River Delta. In March 2014 Alibaba paid HK$5.37 billion for at least 25% of Intime. This year Alibaba CEO Zhang Yong became chairman of Intime Retail and cast it as the "flagship" of online-offline integration, and there are now rumors that the Hong Kong-listed company will be renamed "Alibaba Commerce."

**March 2014: ChinaVision Media**

Before Alibaba used it as a shell and renamed it Alibaba Pictures, ChinaVision had itself gone public in Hong Kong through a backdoor listing. It made films and TV dramas and ran media and wireless new-media businesses, with mediocre results. But since Alibaba bought in and kept pouring its existing sales channel (Taobao Movies) and the quality content it had signed up (Lionsgate, Wasu Media, Huayi Brothers, Enlight Media and others) into the listed company, its market value has swollen tenfold.

**January 2014: CITIC 21CN**

This traditional pharmaceutical company listed in Hong Kong in 1972, and its business volume is unremarkable. But it is the only company in China to hold the first pilot license for third-party online drug sales, and it also controls China's only drug regulatory code system. After investing HK$1.3 billion in early 2014, Alibaba used it as a shell, packed its own future pharmaceutical business into it, and renamed it "Alibaba Health."

**April 2013: Sina Weibo**

Sina Weibo broke away from its parent Sina, a veteran US-listed Chinese stock, and listed on Nasdaq in April 2014. The US$586 million Alibaba had invested earlier, and the advertising Alibaba brought with it, kept the already declining company on a roll for a while: according to the first-quarter results it released in May, ads from Alibaba and major brands made up more than 80% of that quarter's receivables.

**August 2012: Momo**

After only half a year on Nasdaq, Momo announced on June 25 this year that it had received a take-private offer from CEO Tang Yan and its major shareholders. Before the listing, Alibaba had joined several of the social app's funding rounds, investing about US$40 million in total. If Momo does end up listing in China, those investments should prove well worth it.

**January 2010: Shanghai Baozun**

We have written before about Baozun, which runs many brands' Tmall stores on their behalf. It listed on Nasdaq in May 2015, though its market value is modest for now, only US$418 million. In its early funding, Alibaba was its only backer.

**Companies on the road to listing**

February 2015: Meizu. Meizu is not yet listed, but after Alibaba put US$590 million into it as a strategic joint investment in early 2015, it sped up new product development and, like other internet companies, started thinking about raising money. Flyme, the system it developed with Alibaba's YunOS, has had a lukewarm reception, but a new 2-billion-yuan funding round has convinced company president Huang Zhang that Meizu is already worth more than 20 billion yuan.

December 2014: Xiaomi. Among the investors scrambling to hand Xiaomi money, Alibaba's share is very small. In the round at the end of 2014, Yunfeng Capital ranked behind GIC, DST and Hopu Investment. After its latest round, Xiaomi is valued at more than US$40 billion.

April 2013: Kuaidi (now Didi Kuaidi). The taxi-app war, in which Tencent and Alibaba each burned money on subsidies, ended in a marriage between the two giants on Valentine's Day 2015. Since then the company has kept launching new services such as carpooling, designated drivers and even shuttle buses, and if recent reports of a US$2.5 billion injection from China Investment Corporation are confirmed, its valuation will rise to US$15 billion. While Kuaidi Dache ran independently, Alibaba gave it nearly 2.7 billion yuan over four funding rounds.

#### **Tencent's investments in listed companies: 10**

May 2015: Glu Mobile

Tencent paid US$126 million for 14.6% of mobile game developer Glu Mobile Inc, planning to use it to expand into the US game market.

November 2014: Huayi Brothers

In November 2014, Tencent and Alibaba together became Huayi Brothers' second-largest shareholders. One sells the film-finance product Yulebao; the other makes money from online games and from adaptation rights to online-literature IP. Under the cooperation agreement, Huayi must also offer Tencent 5% to 10% of the investment in its films. In other words, Tencent will help finance films too. The three-year agreement, however, gives Tencent distribution rights to only five films.

Still, the same 8.08% stake seems to let Tencent's platforms cut deeper into the film industry. As Zeng Jiaxin, head of marketing for QQ Zone, has put it: we don't just want to promote films; we want to invest in and distribute them too.

September 2014: Sinopec

When state-owned enterprises go online, they are bound to look for big partners. In September 2014 Tencent and 24 other investors put 107.1 billion yuan (about US$17.44 billion) into China's largest state-owned oil company. Each investor could hold up to 2.8%, but Tencent's own amount was not disclosed.

Behind the deal is an energy investment fund called Renbao Tencent Maisheng. As the name suggests, its main sponsors are PICC, Tencent and Maisheng. Sinopec's cooperation with Tencent mainly covers business development and promotion, mobile payment, media publicity, O2O business, map navigation, customer loyalty management, big-data applications and cross-marketing.

August 2014: Wanda E-commerce

Tencent backed e-commerce ventures with commercial real-estate companies twice in one year. In August 2014 it joined Wanda and Baidu to set up a new e-commerce group with 5 billion yuan. Wanda holds 70%, and Tencent and Baidu hold 15% each. Oddly, the group does not sell physical goods; it is meant to sell at-home services. Last year Wanda Plazas drew more than 1.5 billion shopper visits offline, and Tencent and Baidu bring online audiences of a similar size.

March 2014: JD.com

Tencent's stake in China South City convinced many people that investing in JD.com was also a sound move. Two months later, Tencent paid US$214 million for a stake in JD.com and acquired more than 350 million JD.com ordinary shares. The e-commerce and logistics units of QQ Wanggou and Paipai were folded into JD.com, while Tencent's Yixun kept operating as a separate brand. Under the strategic agreement, JD.com also got placement inside WeChat and QQ, Tencent's two highest-traffic social apps.

This year, as the partnership has deepened, JD.com's crowdfunding platform has also proved a good outlet for Tencent's hardware incubation.

March 2014: CJ Games

In March 2014 Tencent paid US$500 million for 28% of Korean game company CJ Games, becoming its third-largest shareholder. CJ Games is in fact a subsidiary of the Korean company CJ E&M. Tencent's mini-game collection *Quanmin Pengpengpeng* came from this studio.

After Tencent bought in, CJ Games also merged with Netmarble, CJ E&M's game publishing arm. With game development and publishing under one roof, it should be easier to drive Tencent's growth in the global mobile game market.

January 2014: China South City

On January 15, 2014, Tencent paid HK$1.5 billion for 9% of China South City. Tencent has kept building out its e-commerce business, and China South City is a property developer whose main businesses are wholesale markets, warehousing and logistics. What Tencent wanted most was probably the logistics.

Tencent also said last year that it would push harder on "micro" O2O services such as "Micro Shopping" and "Micro Life." And China South City's physical outlet-mall business offers useful lessons as Tencent copies Vipshop's flash-sale model. In September 2014 Tencent invested another HK$11.5 billion for 13% of China South City.

June 2014: 58.com

In June 2014 Tencent paid US$736 million for a strategic 19.9% stake in 58.com. After spending US$100 million on more 58.com shares at the end of September, Tencent bought more again through a subsidiary in early October, in a deal worth about US$23 million.

Tencent has an enormous user base and heavy traffic on both PC and mobile. More important, 58.com's users have no social ties to one another, and working with Tencent can bring in Tencent's social connections.

**April 2014: Cheetah Mobile**

In April 2014, on the eve of Cheetah Mobile's US listing, Baidu joined Kingsoft and Xiaomi in buying shares in the company. The three together subscribed for up to US$50 million in shares, of which Baidu spent US$20 million.

After this round, Cheetah's shareholders were all giants of Chinese tech, including Tencent, Xiaomi and Baidu, with Tencent the second-largest shareholder.

**April 2014: Weebly**

In April 2014 Tencent invested US$35 million in Weebly, a website-building tool for businesses. For a while Weebly's valuation was talked up to US$455 million. That autumn Weebly went public, raising US$127 million in its IPO.

Tencent mainly took this clean, simple site builder and offered it to the merchants on its e-commerce platform. If you remember how alike WeChat micro-business storefronts all looked, you will understand. That is Weebly's biggest market in China.

**Companies on the road to listing**

Dianping. Starting in February 2014, Tencent invested US$400 million for 20% of Dianping, though the product still runs independently. Of course, you can also find ways into it from WeChat and QQ. Since taking Tencent's money, Dianping has been locked in a spending contest with group-buying sites such as Meituan. At the end of 2014 Dianping planned an IPO to raise at least 200 million. So far, though, it has not managed to list.

Snapchat. Though it already owned WeChat and QQ, China's two biggest social platforms, Tencent also took part in the US$60 million Series B round of Snapchat, the disappearing-message social app, in June 2013. It was not a large investment. Snapchat, which has been talking about going public since 2014, finally filed its IPO plan this May.

Kuaidi (now Didi Kuaidi). The taxi-app war, in which Tencent and Alibaba each burned money on subsidies, ended in a marriage between the two giants on Valentine's Day 2015. Since then the company has kept launching new services such as carpooling, designated drivers and even shuttle buses, and if recent reports of a US$2.5 billion injection from China Investment Corporation are confirmed, its valuation will rise to US$15 billion. While Kuaidi Dache ran independently, Alibaba gave it nearly 2.7 billion yuan over four funding rounds.

Sogou. On September 16, 2013, Tencent paid US$448 million for a stake in Sogou. Its Soso search engine and QQ input-method businesses were merged with Sogou's existing operations to form a new Sogou. According to Bloomberg, Sogou plans a US IPO at a valuation of about US$3 billion, as early as the second half of this year.

Aiming. On March 25 this year, the Japanese game company Aiming announced that it would list on the Tokyo Stock Exchange because it needed more money to develop new games. In December 2014 Aiming had taken an investment from Tencent, the first Japanese game developer Tencent backed. Their cooperation centers mainly on publishing: Tencent will publish Aiming's games in mainland China, Hong Kong and Macau, and Aiming will bring Tencent's games to Japan.

Tongcheng. Tongcheng says that investors including Wanda and Tencent have signaled interest in its new funding round and will support Tongcheng Travel in an independent IPO on China's capital market, and that it has recently formally begun its A-share IPO. Last April Trip.com Group made a strategic investment of more than US$200 million in Tongcheng, becoming its second-largest shareholder after the management team with a stake of about 30%. Tencent, through two investments starting last June, holds about 15%, making it Tongcheng Travel's third-largest shareholder.

#### **Baidu's investments in listed companies: 4**

**June 2015: SMI Holdings**

Of the listed companies Baidu has invested in, SMI Holdings is the only one that is purely an entertainment and media business. Its main business is running offline movie theaters, which has little to do with internet services.

This June, Baidu, together with Tianan Property Insurance and Hopu Investment, paid HK$450 million for 4.8% of SMI's issued shares. So far we have seen no change in strategy at either company since Baidu bought in.

**August 2014: Wanda E-commerce**

Last August Baidu joined Wanda and Tencent to set up an e-commerce group with 5 billion yuan. Wanda holds 70%, and Baidu and Tencent hold 15% each. Oddly, the group does not sell physical goods; it is meant to sell at-home services. Last year Wanda Plazas drew more than 1.5 billion shopper visits offline, and Tencent and Baidu bring online audiences of a similar size.

**April 2014: Cheetah Mobile**

In April 2014, on the eve of Cheetah Mobile's US listing, Baidu joined Kingsoft and Xiaomi in buying shares in the company. The three together subscribed for up to US$50 million in shares, of which Baidu spent US$20 million.

After this round, Cheetah's shareholders were all giants of Chinese tech, including Tencent, Xiaomi and Baidu, with Tencent the second-largest shareholder.

June 2011: Qunar

The online travel site Qunar was closer to an acquisition. As early as 2011, Baidu paid US$306 million for 60% of Qunar, which valued Qunar at US$483 million. Qunar was then one of China's largest travel-product websites and was even rumored to be planning an IPO, but in the end it chose not to list and let Baidu take control instead. It was Baidu's largest strategic investment up to that point.

Afterward, Baidu folded Qunar's travel search results into Baidu's own travel search, while Qunar used the money to build hotel search and mobile apps. On November 1, 2013, two years after Baidu's big investment, Qunar listed on Nasdaq and closed its first day worth US$3.19 billion, which put Baidu's stake at US$926 million. On paper, Baidu's investment had more than tripled by the time Qunar went public.

**Companies on the road to listing**

Baixing.com. In June 2015 Baidu invested 200 million yuan in Baixing.com, a local classified-ads site. Next to the industry's two biggest sites, Ganji and 58.com, Baixing is only second-tier. But the first-tier players, 58.com, Ganji and Dianping, had all already taken money from Tencent, and 58.com and Ganji merged this year. Baixing was in a sense Baidu's only option. Within a month of the investment news, Baixing had unwound its VIE structure and was preparing to list in China.

Uber. In December 2014 Baidu made a US$600 million strategic investment in the American ride-hailing app Uber, its biggest single investment in recent years. When Uber's Series D round closed, Baidu owned 1.5% of the company.

Hujiang. Hujiang, an online education site founded in 2001, took US$80 million from Baidu in April 2014. It is among the oldest and largest online education sites in China and now has more than 80 million users.

## Where Have the Three Been Investing Over the Past Six Months?

Tally up the three companies' investments in the first half of this year and you find them concentrated in four areas: mobility, car trading, social, games and e-commerce.

**Mobility**

Tencent's backing of Kuaidi and Alibaba's backing of Didi drove China's taxi-app war of 2013. In 2014, as Uber entered China, premium car-hailing, which bypasses traditional taxis, became a profitable direction. Didi and Kuaidi each launched their own premium car services and announced their merger in February this year. After the merger, Tencent and Alibaba stepped up their investment, and in July, together with Ping An and other institutions, they injected US$2 billion into Didi Kuaidi.

Baidu, which had missed the taxi war, made a US$600 million strategic investment at the end of last year in Uber, the pioneer of ride-hailing apps. When Uber's Series D round closed, Baidu owned 1.5% of the company.

At the time, Didi Dache had just raised US$700 million, with Tencent as a key strategic investor, while Kuaidi Dache had Alibaba behind it supplying traffic and promotion. Baidu CEO Robin Li said the Uber deal was not a financial investment; what Baidu valued was the strategic partnership. Soon afterward, Uber switched its maps in China to Baidu's and added Baidu Wallet as a payment option, while Baidu added an Uber ride-hailing option to its own maps.

Recently, Uber CEO Travis Kalanick confirmed in an interview that Uber would set up a local company in China, though it is not yet clear whether Baidu will be the partner. Hard on the heels of the Uber deal, Baidu also announced investments in two carpooling apps, 51 Yongche and Tiantian Yongche, in April this year.

**Car trading**

This Tuesday, the used-car e-commerce platform Renrenche announced a US$85 million Series C round led by Tencent. According to a 2014 report from the automotive research firm J.D. Power, 4S dealerships' income from after-sales service is shrinking sharply, even as the after-sales market grew by 37.3 billion yuan in 2014.

The companies grabbing that market are exactly these internet services. Since the start of this year, Tencent, Baidu and Alibaba have all clearly stepped up their investment in the auto aftermarket.

In February Tencent and JD.com invested 1.3 billion in Bitauto and struck a strategic partnership that includes used-car trading. Of that, 750 million in exclusive resources comes mainly from JD.com, which will provide an e-commerce platform for car sales. In return, Bitauto, listed on the NYSE since 2010, will open up its auto database, including car prices, market conditions and model data.

Then in March, Baidu led a US$170 million Series C round for the used-car trading platform Youxinpai. Interestingly, besides the used-car services on its own site, Bitauto, through CEO Li Bin, also invested in Youxinpai in 2011. And Tencent had already bought in at Youxinpai's Series A.

Alibaba has its own e-commerce platform. In February it too announced that it would merge the used-car trading platform it launched at the end of 2014 with its local auto services business.

Why are they all betting on used-car trading platforms? A J.D. Power analyst told QDaily: "Unlike other parts of after-sales, used-car trading is an auto aftermarket where revenue comes quickly as transaction volume grows. It also brings in car loans and car insurance."

**Social**

With its latest update, Alipay looks more and more like WeChat. Taobao Wangwang, once the object of high hopes, was renamed AliWangwang and still works only as a chat tool for online shopping. Laiwang has ended up as an internal messaging tool for Alibaba staff. In 2015 Alibaba nonetheless invested US$200 million in Snapchat, the disappearing-message chat app. In September 2013 Tencent had also taken part in Snapchat's US$80 million Series B.

Neither sum is large. Beyond the financial return, both Tencent and Alibaba seem to be hoping Snapchat will come to China. Tencent already owns China's two big messaging apps, WeChat and QQ, yet in the first half of this year it still invested in two mobile social apps, Same and Whisper. Like Snapchat, both are homegrown anonymous social apps.

When Pony Ma invested in Same, he said he could not see much potential in it, but that it had a feel of the future. And now the mobile QQ app has a private "whisper" feature too.

**Games**

More people are playing games on their phones, and this year Tencent and Alibaba invested in a batch of mobile game studios and publishers.

Meanwhile Tencent's most profitable business, games, is expanding quickly overseas. Through an investment in February, Tencent is now the largest shareholder of Miniclip, the Swiss online game company. Miniclip makes mobile games; you may have played its pool game, 8 Ball Pool.

In May Tencent paid US$126 million for 14.6% of mobile game developer Glu Mobile Inc. This veteran American game maker still relies mainly on the role-playing game *Kim Kardashian: Hollywood*.

That same month, the American mobile game developer Pocket Gems took US$60 million from Tencent. What Tencent gets is little more than the rights to publish overseas games in China.

Alibaba, for its part, this year combined forces with UC 9Game, which it had invested in earlier, to launch a mobile game platform.

**E-commerce**

As China's largest e-commerce platform, Alibaba is turning abroad for its next e-commerce investments.

The latest came on August 3, when Alibaba confirmed its investment in the Indian e-commerce company Snapdeal. The round raised US$500 million, and other investors included SoftBank and Foxconn. India is becoming one of the most active e-commerce markets in the world.

Jet, an e-commerce upstart taking on Amazon, is also on Alibaba's investment list, though neither side has yet responded to the report. Baidu's and Tencent's directions are clear too. Since Alibaba already holds the general e-commerce market, both are looking for more specialized e-commerce, or reaching deeper into e-commerce logistics management.

This July, MissFresh announced a major Pre-A investment from Tencent, though it did not disclose the amount. Tencent, better placed to enter e-commerce through social networking, has never turned that traffic into sales well enough. Fresh produce is a newly emerging field, and Tencent wants to try it too. What if it turns out to be a dark horse?

Baidu, meanwhile, spent US$10 million on a stake in Baichuan Kuaixian oTMS, a service provider for the freight and transportation industry. Baidu might put this kind of logistics management to use in mobility, food delivery and even e-commerce. What e-commerce? Last year Baidu set up Wanda E-commerce with Wanda and Tencent. Then again, the new company mainly sells at-home services.
